questions.prompt: What does the @api decorator mark on an LWC component's class?
options: A property or method that is part of the component's public interface, settable or callable by a parent component
A field that must be mutated in place rather than reassigned
A method that runs automatically on every render of the component
An event listener bound directly in the template
A getter that can never be referenced from the template
A field that is encrypted when stored on the client
questions.explain: @api marks a property or method as part of a component's public API -- a parent is allowed to set or read an @api property, or call an @api method, directly.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a confusion with @track, not @api. @api is about exposing a property or method publicly to a parent; it has nothing to do with whether the field is mutated in place versus reassigned, which is the @track/reactivity distinction covered in Lesson 6.

questions.prompt: A component has fields `price` and `quantity`, and a getter `get lineTotal() { return this.price * this.quantity; }`. After `this.quantity` changes, what has to happen for `lineTotal` to show the correct new value in the template?
options: Nothing extra -- the getter recomputes fresh whenever it's read, and the framework re-renders anything depending on it automatically once quantity changes
A separate method must manually recompute and reassign lineTotal as a field
The component must call this.render() explicitly
lineTotal must be decorated with @track for the change to be picked up
questions.explain: A getter is computed fresh every time it's read, so there's no separate value to keep in sync -- once quantity (a reactive field referenced by the getter) changes, the framework re-renders anything depending on lineTotal automatically.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about reactivity in LWC, per this course.
options: Reassigning a whole field to a new value (e.g. this.count = this.count + 1) is observed automatically, with no decorator required
@track is still needed to observe a mutation to a property inside an existing object or an element inside an existing array
@api properties can be reassigned freely by the child component itself as a normal part of the component's design
Reassigning a field to an entirely new object (e.g. this.address = {...this.address, city: 'X'}) is reactive without needing @track
@track makes a field settable by a parent component
questions.explain: Plain reassignment is reactive by default (no decorator needed). @track is specifically for observing in-place mutation of an object's properties or an array's elements. Reassigning to a brand-new object is also reactive without @track. @api properties are meant to be set by the parent and read (not reassigned) by the child, and @track has nothing to do with making a field settable by a parent -- that's @api's job.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every LWC HTML template file must start and end with a single root ________ element.
questions.explain: Every LWC template file wraps all of its markup inside exactly one root <template> tag -- never raw HTML outside it, and never multiple sibling root elements.

questions.prompt: Match each LWC template directive or concept to what it actually does.
right: Exposes first and last booleans for the current item in a list
The modern multi-branch directive set for conditional rendering
The unique, stable identifier the framework uses to track list items across re-renders
The standard directive for rendering a simple list of items
questions.explain: lwc:if/elseif/else is the modern conditional-rendering directive chain. for:each is the standard list-rendering directive. iterator: does the same job as for:each but also exposes first/last booleans. key is the stable identifier the framework uses to correctly track, reuse, and reorder list items across re-renders.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating and deploying a brand-new LWC component via the Salesforce CLI in the correct order.
items: Run sf project generate to scaffold a new Salesforce DX project
Run sf org login web to authorize a Developer Edition org
Run sf lightning generate component to scaffold a new component bundle
Run sf project deploy start to push the code to the org
questions.explain: The project must exist before anything else (sf project generate), then the org needs to be authorized (sf org login web), then a component bundle is scaffolded inside the project (sf lightning generate component), and finally the code is deployed to the authorized org (sf project deploy start).

questions.prompt: A child component dispatches a custom event named `statusChange`. Why might a parent's listener attribute `onstatusChange={handler}` fail to work as expected?
options: Custom events cannot carry a detail payload
Custom event names (and their listener attributes) must be lowercase, since HTML attributes are case-insensitive -- it should be dispatched as 'statuschange' and listened for as 'onstatuschange'
Event listeners can only be attached to base Lightning components, not custom ones
The event must be dispatched from connectedCallback() specifically
questions.explain: Because HTML attributes are case-insensitive, mixed-case event names like statusChange are indistinguishable from their lowercase form to a listener -- the platform convention requires lowercase, single-word event names to avoid this ambiguity entirely.

questions.prompt: A grandchild component needs to notify a grandparent two levels up in the component tree. Why doesn't a plain, non-bubbling CustomEvent reach the grandparent automatically?
options: CustomEvents can only be dispatched once per component instance

A plain CustomEvent only reaches a listener attached directly to the dispatching element -- the intermediate component would need to catch it and re-dispatch its own event, or the design should use Lightning Message Service instead
Grandchildren are not allowed to dispatch events in LWC
Events automatically bubble through exactly two levels, but no more
questions.explain: Without bubbles/composed set, a CustomEvent is only visible to a listener on the exact dispatching element. Reaching two levels up requires either explicit re-dispatching at each intermediate layer, or using Lightning Message Service for components that aren't closely related in the tree.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lightning Message Service (LMS).
options: LMS lets components with no parent-child relationship communicate, including across LWC, Aura, and Visualforce
A Lightning Message Channel is defined in a .messageChannel-meta.xml file
Wiring MessageContext manages the message context's lifecycle automatically, unlike calling createMessageContext() directly
A subscription created in connectedCallback() should be released in disconnectedCallback() to avoid it outliving the component
LMS can only be used between two LWC components, never Aura or Visualforce
questions.explain: LMS exists specifically for unrelated components, including across LWC, Aura, and Visualforce -- the last option directly contradicts that. Message channels are defined via .messageChannel-meta.xml, wiring MessageContext simplifies lifecycle management, and pairing subscribe/unsubscribe with connectedCallback/disconnectedCallback prevents a stale subscription from outliving its component.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the lifecycle hook that fires when a component is removed from the DOM, and is the standard place to unsubscribe from a message channel or clear a timer, is called ________.
questions.explain: disconnectedCallback() fires when a component is removed from the DOM, making it the standard place for cleanup such as unsubscribing from a Lightning Message Channel or clearing a timer or interval.

questions.prompt: Match each LWC lifecycle hook to what it's actually used for.
right: Fires when an unhandled error occurs in the component or a child
Runs before the component is attached to the DOM; cannot access this.template or attributes yet
Fires after every render; needs a guard to avoid triggering itself repeatedly
Fires when the component is inserted into the DOM; can fire more than once per instance
questions.explain: constructor() runs before DOM attachment, with strict limits on what it can touch. connectedCallback() fires on DOM insertion and can fire again if the component is reattached. renderedCallback() fires after every render and needs a guard for one-time logic. errorCallback() fires specifically on an unhandled error in the component or a descendant.

questions.prompt: Put these LWC lifecycle events in the order they occur for a component being created, rendered, and later removed.
items: constructor() runs
connectedCallback() runs
renderedCallback() runs after the first render
disconnectedCallback() runs when the component is removed
questions.explain: A component's class instance is created first (constructor), then it's attached to the DOM (connectedCallback), then its template renders and renderedCallback fires, and finally, if the component is later removed from the DOM, disconnectedCallback runs for cleanup.

questions.prompt: What does marking an Apex method @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) declare about that method?
options: It is read-only and safe for the client to cache, and it is also a requirement for using the method with @wire
It automatically runs asynchronously on a background thread
It bypasses field-level security for the running user
It allows the method to perform DML as long as the DML happens inside a try/catch block
It makes the method callable only from Aura, never from LWC
It doubles the method's governor limit for SOQL queries
questions.explain: cacheable=true declares a method read-only and safe to cache on the client, which is also a hard requirement for using that method with @wire, since the wire service relies on being able to cache and reuse results.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D is the common confusion: cacheable=true specifically means the method has no side effects, so it can never perform DML, regardless of try/catch. A method with DML must be called imperatively instead, exactly because it cannot be marked cacheable=true.

questions.prompt: A component needs to fetch contacts in response to a 'Load More' button click, where the user may click it several times. Which approach, and why?
options: @wire the Apex method with a reactive parameter, since @wire automatically handles repeated calls
Call the Apex method imperatively from the button's click handler, since this is a user-triggered action rather than data that should load automatically or refresh on a reactive parameter change
The method cannot be called at all unless it is cacheable=true
Use Lightning Message Service to trigger the Apex call
questions.explain: A user-triggered, repeatable action like a 'Load More' click is exactly the case for an imperative call -- @wire is for data that should load automatically and refresh via reactive parameters, not for direct responses to a specific click.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about refreshing data after a write, per this course.
options: refreshApex() requires storing the entire wire result object (data and error), not just result.data, to work correctly
notifyRecordUpdateAvailable() refreshes LDS's cache for specific record Ids across every component using them
getRecordNotifyChange() is the current recommended function and should always be used over notifyRecordUpdateAvailable()
If a record changes entirely through LDS's own write functions (like updateRecord), no extra refresh call is needed for other getRecord-wired components
Imperative Apex writes automatically refresh any separately wired custom Apex read with no extra code
questions.explain: refreshApex() needs the whole stored wire result. notifyRecordUpdateAvailable() refreshes LDS's cache for specific records across components. LDS's own shared cache already keeps getRecord-wired components in sync after an LDS write, with no extra call needed. getRecordNotifyChange() is deprecated, not recommended, and imperative Apex writes do NOT automatically refresh a separately wired custom Apex read -- that's exactly the gap these tools close.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an Apex method named `getAccounts` on a class named `AccountController` is imported into LWC with the path '@salesforce/apex/________'.
questions.explain: The import path always follows @salesforce/apex/ClassName.methodName -- here, AccountController.getAccounts, with exact casing matching the Apex class and method.

questions.prompt: Match each Lightning Data Service function from lightning/uiRecordApi to what it does.
right: Removes a record given its Id
A wire adapter that reads a record's field data
Changes fields on an existing record, given its Id and the fields to change
Creates a new record, given an object API name and a fields map
questions.explain: getRecord is the wire adapter for reading record data. createRecord makes a new record from an apiName and fields map. updateRecord changes an existing record's fields given its Id. deleteRecord removes a record given just its Id. The three write functions are all called imperatively, never wired.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a standard imperative Apex save-with-toast flow in the correct order.
items: Call the imperative Apex method inside a try block, awaiting its result
On success, dispatch a ShowToastEvent with variant 'success'
If the call throws, catch the error in the catch block
Extract a readable message (e.g. error.body.message) and dispatch a ShowToastEvent with variant 'error'
questions.explain: The call is attempted first inside try/await. If it succeeds, a success toast is dispatched. If it throws, the catch block receives the error, and only then is a readable message extracted and shown as an error toast -- error extraction only makes sense after an error has actually been caught.

questions.prompt: Before building a custom input field from raw HTML, what does this course recommend checking first, and why?
options: Whether a base Lightning component (like lightning-input) already covers the need, since base components already handle SLDS styling and accessibility concerns that would otherwise have to be redone by hand
Whether the field needs to be marked @track
Whether the org has any custom Apex classes deployed
Whether the component needs a .svg icon file
questions.explain: Base Lightning components already handle SLDS styling and accessibility (ARIA attributes, keyboard behavior) -- checking for an existing base component before hand-building the same control avoids redoing that work yourself.

questions.prompt: A parent needs to override a child's default background color without the child exposing a new @api property. What is the sanctioned mechanism for this across the shadow DOM boundary?
options: The parent should target the child's internal class names directly, such as .slds-input

A CSS custom property (like --badge-color), which the child defines with a fallback and the parent sets on the child's tag -- custom properties are a documented exception that inherit through shadow DOM
The :host selector, used from the parent's own CSS file
Shadow DOM blocks all styling crossing component boundaries with no exceptions, so this isn't possible
questions.explain: CSS custom properties are the documented exception that inherits through shadow DOM, letting a parent influence a child's styling without the child needing a new @api property, and without the parent reaching into classes it doesn't own.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SLDS and component styling, per this course.
options: SLDS utility classes can be passed into a base component's class attribute, adding alongside the component's own internal classes
Starting at LWC API version 61.0, double-dash class names like slds-p-around--small became single-underscore names like slds-p-around_small
It is safe and recommended to target a base component's internal classes, like .slds-input, directly from outside the component
A component's own .css file is automatically scoped to just that component, with no special naming convention required
lightning-layout and lightning-layout-item expose some, but not all, SLDS grid variations through their own attributes
questions.explain: Utility classes are additive on base components. The double-dash-to-underscore change happened at API v61.0. Component CSS is automatically scoped via shadow DOM. Layout components expose common grid settings through attributes but not every grid class. Targeting a base component's internal classes directly is explicitly discouraged, since those internals aren't a documented public contract and can change without warning.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a static resource named `companyLogo` is imported into a component with the path '@salesforce/________/companyLogo'.
questions.explain: Static resources are imported as URLs through the path @salesforce/resourceUrl/ResourceName, where the name must exactly match the static resource's name in Setup.

questions.prompt: Match each Lightning App Builder target to what it makes a component available on.
right: A custom Lightning Home page
Restricts a lightning__RecordPage component to specific object types
A record detail page, such as Account or Case
A custom Lightning app page, independent of any specific record
questions.explain: lightning__RecordPage targets record detail pages. lightning__AppPage targets custom app pages. lightning__HomePage targets custom Home pages. The <objects> element, nested inside a lightning__RecordPage targetConfig, restricts which object's record pages the component is offered on.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of making a component's property admin-configurable in Lightning App Builder in a correct working order.
items: Set isExposed to true in the component's js-meta.xml
Add the relevant <target> (e.g. lightning__RecordPage) to the js-meta.xml
Declare the property as @api on the component's JavaScript class
Add a matching <property> entry inside a <targetConfig> for that target
questions.explain: A component must first be exposed at all (isExposed true) and assigned at least one target before targetConfigs for that target are meaningful. The @api property must exist on the class, and the targetConfig's <property> entry must match it by name to actually surface it as an admin-configurable field.

questions.prompt: Why does a search-as-you-type feature typically need debouncing before calling Apex?
options: Because Apex methods cannot accept string parameters

Because calling Apex on every keystroke would trigger several wasted server round trips, most immediately superseded by the next one -- debouncing waits for a short pause before actually firing the call
Because @wire automatically debounces every call with no configuration
Because debouncing is required by the LWC compiler for any imperative call
questions.explain: Without debouncing, typing a word could trigger several server calls in quick succession, most of them wasted because they're immediately superseded by the next keystroke's call -- debouncing waits for a pause before firing.

questions.prompt: Why does an unguarded property assignment inside renderedCallback() risk becoming both a correctness bug and a performance problem?
options: renderedCallback() only ever runs once, so this isn't actually a real risk

renderedCallback() runs after every render, so an unguarded assignment can trigger another render (correctness risk of an infinite loop) and, even short of that, repeats costly work on every render (performance risk)
renderedCallback() cannot read or write any component properties at all
Property assignments are not allowed inside any lifecycle hook
questions.explain: Because renderedCallback() fires after every render, an unguarded property assignment can trigger another render (risking an infinite loop) and, even without a full loop, unconditionally repeats expensive work on every single render -- a boolean guard addresses both risks.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about accessibility in LWC, per this course.
options: Base Lightning components automatically update their own ARIA attributes as their state changes
aria-label should be used instead of visible text whenever possible, as the first choice
slds-assistive-text visually hides content while keeping it announced by screen readers, unlike display: none
The visible focus indicator should never be removed with CSS, since it's how keyboard-only users track their position
Tab order should generally be forced with tabindex rather than following natural DOM order
questions.explain: Base components manage their own ARIA state automatically. slds-assistive-text hides content visually while keeping it available to screen readers. The focus indicator must never be removed. Visible text is the documented first choice over aria-label, not the other way around, and DOM order -- not forced tabindex -- should drive tab order.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the function imported from the 'lwc' module that creates a testable instance of a component in a Jest test is called ________.
questions.explain: createElement, imported from the lwc module itself (not from the component), creates a testable instance of the component, given its tag name and the imported class via the is option.

questions.prompt: Match each performance problem from this course to its standard fix.
left: Rendering thousands of rows directly into the DOM at once
Expensive work running unconditionally inside renderedCallback()
Fetching data once per row instead of once per list
A getter doing expensive filtering/sorting, read on every frequent re-render
right: Cache the derived result in a plain field, recomputed only when its real inputs change
Fetch everything the list needs in one batched call and pass it down to children
Pagination or server-side lazy loading, rather than rendering the full result set at once
A boolean guard ensuring one-time logic only runs once
questions.explain: Large lists need pagination or lazy loading rather than rendering everything at once. Unconditional renderedCallback() work needs a guard. Per-row fetching should be replaced with one batched fetch distributed to children. An expensive, frequently-read getter should have its result cached in a plain field recomputed only when its actual inputs change.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the standard LWC Jest test pattern in the correct order.
items: Import createElement from 'lwc' and the component class from its module
Create the element with createElement and optionally set @api properties on it
Append the element to document.body so it actually renders
Query the rendered result through element.shadowRoot.querySelector and assert on it
questions.explain: The test first imports what it needs, then creates the element (optionally configuring its public properties before it renders), then attaches it to the DOM so rendering actually happens, and only then queries the rendered shadow DOM to make assertions -- nothing is rendered, and nothing can be meaningfully queried, until the element is appended.
